newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-FOCUS-Telstra rings Australian record profit.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-FOCUS-Telstra rings Australian record profit.

text.p: Australian state-owned telecommunications carrier Telstra Corp rang up a national record profit on Friday, but immediately unveiled plans to start shedding almost a third of its staff ahead of privatisation.
Telstra's annual 1995/96 (July-June) net profit jumped 31.5 percent to A$2.3 billion, surpassing the National Australia Bank as corporate Australia's biggest earner.
"It's a very encouraging result for Telstra because it says we are up to making real progress and becoming more productive and henceforth competitive," chief executive Frank Blount said.

But the announcement comes as Telstra finds itself at the centre of a political storm over the conservative government's plan to sell a third of the carrier, once widely considered to be a "sacred cow" of Australia's state assets.
In preparation for its part privatisation, Telstra announced at a news conference here on Friday it would cut its staff of roughly 76,000 by 22,000 jobs over the next three fiscal years.
"It is critical that the corporation continues to make efficiency gains and, indeed, accelerates these gains, if we are to compete effectively with our global and domestic competitors," Blount said.

Telstra has already said it will cut 9,000 jobs in 1996/97 and announced on Friday it would slash another 13,000 jobs in the following two years. In 1996/97 alone, it has set aside A$1.1 billion to pay for the redundancy programme.

The announcement follows suggestions from stock market analysts that Telstra needs to lay off roughly a third of its staff to boost its efficiency to international benchmarks and guarantee the best return to the government from privatisation.
"If it's not earning the biggest profit then Australians are entitled to ask 'why not?'...It's single biggest hurdle is labour productivity," a Sydney-based analyst told Reuters.
Telstra's huge staff numbers put it among the least productive of the world's 15 top carriers, he added.
Anticipating resistence to the cuts, Blount told the news conference that trade unions had been warned of the move.
"We know they're not happy about it. By the way our staff are not particularly happy about it either but...we don't have a choice, we have to drive forward," Blount said.

The issue of staff cuts is among a number of concerns cited by opponents to government plans to raise an estimated A$8 billion from the part-sale of Telstra, which faces a rocky passage through the upper house of parliament.
But Communications Minister Richard Alston denied on Friday that the job losses were related to the partial sale.
"What is happening now is not privatisation related," Alston told reporters in the capital, Canberra.

The opposition Labor Party and an influential minor party, the Australian Democrats, oppose the privatisation, leaving Telstra's fate in the hands of independent senators who will effectively have a casting vote in the upper house.
One of the senators has proposed the sale go ahead without the government relinquishing any control of Telstra, by way of an issue of redeemable preference shares to private investors.
These type of shares are in effect a form of debt and give holders less influence than ordinary, voting shareholders.
